newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany cautiously hopes river flood dikes can hold.
newsitem.headline: Germany cautiously hopes river flood dikes can hold.

text.p: German authorities saw a shimmer of hope on Monday that dikes along the swollen Oder River could be kept from bursting but stressed that the water-logged flood barriers were not yet fully secure.

Germany's biggest industrial group, Daimler-Benz AG, announced plans to grant one million marks ($537,000) for flood victims during a benefit programme broadcast by the public television network ARD on Sunday night.

German soldiers and volunteers worked feverishly to bolster the dikes on the Oder and repair new fissures in the dike near the village of Hohenwutzen, the focus of rescue activities in the Oderbruch basin on Germany's eastern border.
"The Oderbruch region remains our greatest concern," said Brandenburg state premier Manfred Stolpe during the ARD broadcast.
Helicopters flew tonnes of sand and gravel to weak spots in the dike in the Oderbruch near Hohenwutzen, Reitwein and Zollbruecke, where soldiers have toiled day and night to save the dike.

Should the dike break, which officials said was still possible, water would inundate the Oderbruch, an area 17 km (11 miles) wide and 50 km (30 miles) long on Germany's frontier with Poland, engulfing villages, farms and factories.

Germany has escaped the worst of a month of flooding from torrential rains in east-central Europe that killed more than 100 people in Poland and the Czech Republic. But damage to German homes, businesses and farms has been extensive.

As Oder water levels began falling over the weekend, officials became optimistic for the first time that more than 10,000 soldiers and thousands more volunteer aid workers and local residents could succeed in holding back the flood.
Officials have repeatedly cautioned that the chances of a break in the dike were still high because the rain-gorged river continued to press against the weakened dikes.
Matthias Platzek, Brandenburg environment minister, said the river needed to fall some one and a half metres (five feet) before the dikes could be deemed safe.
The Brandenburg interior ministry said the river was receding at a rate of half a cm each hour, which meant it would still be days before officials could signal the all clear.
The ministry added, however, that further south in the main regional town of Frankfurt an der Oder, sandbag barriers that had defended it from flood tides had now been removed.
Soldiers erecting a series of secondary dikes near Reitwein in the Oderbruch encountered an unexpected complication when they uncovered 10 unexploded bombs from the Second World War.
The ministry said the entire area needed to be searched for more bombs before work on the dikes could continue. ($ = 1.861 German Marks)
